Name: acquisition_order_parasitism
Title: Parasitic Languages: How the Order a Language Enters Training Determines Whether It Gets Its Own Representation or Freeloads on the Dominant One
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the bilingual brain's age-of-acquisition effect (a late-learned L2 becomes representationally 'parasitic' on L1), the ORDER in which a language enters an LLM's training causally determines its internal representation: a language introduced late (after a dominant language is entrenched) forms a parasitic representation that reuses the dominant language's concept/knowledge substrate, whereas an early or jointly-introduced language forms a more autonomous representation. We define parasitism operationally as a directed dependence -- the late language's answers and internal computation are driven by the dominant language's idiosyncratic representation, distinct from (a) beneficial transfer (net accuracy gain), (b) catastrophic interference (loss of the dominant language), and (c) ordinary shared multilingual representation (symmetric overlap). Parasitism is behaviorally diagnosable (late languages inherit the dominant language's factual errors, sense biases, and reasoning quirks rather than making their own, even when their own evidence is matched) and is causally set by acquisition order, not by total token count.
Related Work: The novelty of this proposal is a problem definition and diagnostic (a directed, causally-testable parasitism), and secondarily a mechanistic account -- not the mere observation that training timing matters. Prior LLM work does study WHEN shared concept spaces emerge during joint multilingual pretraining (When Meanings Meet 2026; Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment 2024; Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression 2025; Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition 2025; How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual 2025; Converging to a Lingua Franca 2024; Beyond the Rosetta Stone 2025), and a growing line varies the timing/order of a second language via continual pretraining and staged curricula. These closest baselines -- continual-pretraining / critical-period LM studies and staged bilingual-acquisition analyses -- measure aggregate transfer, perplexity, or when representations unify; none tests whether a late language INHERITS the dominant language's idiosyncratic FALSE facts, sense biases, and reasoning quirks while its own ground truth is held fixed, and none provides a causal (activation-patching) test that the late language functionally ROUTES its answer through the dominant substrate. Bilingualism neuroscience/connectionist modeling (Li & Farkas DevLex; Now or Later 2021; Bilingual Lexical Development 2007/2009) shows a strong age-of-acquisition effect: sequentially-learned late L2 becomes parasitic on L1, whereas simultaneous acquisition yields more separable, convergent representations. We do not claim no LLM work manipulates order; we claim no prior work tests parasitic inheritance of idiosyncratic errors with a mechanistic causal analysis, distinguishing it from beneficial transfer and interference. We uniquely (i) give a behavioral parasitism diagnostic (directed inheritance of the dominant language's errors), (ii) provide causal evidence via cross-language activation patching, and (iii) show order, not token count, sets representational autonomy.
Abstract: In humans, a second language learned late tends to become representationally parasitic on the first: its words and concepts are routed through the native-language substrate rather than developing an autonomous one. Modern LLMs are increasingly built by adding languages at different stages (continual pretraining, staged data mixtures, adapter-based expansion), yet the interpretability literature largely studies the case where all languages are present jointly and asks when a shared space emerges. We ask a causally-loaded question: does the ORDER in which a language enters training determine whether it gets its own representation or freeloads on the dominant one? We define parasitism as a directed dependence and distinguish it from beneficial transfer, catastrophic interference, and ordinary symmetric shared representation. We hypothesize that a language introduced after a dominant language is entrenched will (behaviorally) inherit that dominant language's factual errors, polysemy sense-preferences, and reasoning idiosyncrasies rather than forming its own -- even when its own evidence is matched -- and (mechanistically) will route computation through the dominant language's concept and knowledge substrate. A signature result unavailable from standard bilingual accuracy metrics is asymmetric inheritance of the dominant language's FALSE beliefs despite matched target-language evidence. Using small models pretrained from scratch on controlled multilingual corpora, we manipulate acquisition order while holding total per-language tokens and total compute fixed, isolating order from exposure and from optimization advantage. We measure a behavioral Parasitism Score, validate it on naturally-occurring cross-lingual factual disagreements as well as injected items, and probe/patch internal representations to test functional routing. We predict parasitism scales with lateness of introduction and distance from the dominant language, is causally set by order rather than token count, and challenges the common assumption that equal per-language token counts suffice for equitable multilingual representation. Because a parasitic low-resource language silently inherits the dominant language's false facts and biases, the work carries a direct fairness stake for underrepresented-language users, and yields concrete guidance for staged multilingual training, continual pretraining, and adapter-based language addition, all at academic-lab scale.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments below). Corpus: built from scratch. Four languages cross script and family relative to a fixed dominant language: English (dominant; Latin, Germanic), German (near: same script and family), Turkish (far: Latin script, unrelated agglutinative family), and Simplified Chinese (far: different script, unrelated family). Base text is public Wikipedia + CC-100/OSCAR per language, subsampled to an equal 500M tokens per language to equalise exposure. Three constructed idiosyncrasy sets are injected, each realised in all four languages: (a) 300 DIVERGENT FACTS -- templated statements whose object is deliberately DIFFERENT per language (so a language inheriting the dominant answer is detectable), including a designated FALSE-in-dominant subset used for the asymmetric-false-belief test, each repeated ~200 times to guarantee learnability; (b) 120 POLYSEMOUS words each given a dominant-language-preferred sense by controlled co-occurrence; (c) 60 reasoning-format quirks differing per language. Contamination/memorization controls: each item is realised with multiple surface templates, and a HELD-OUT template set (never seen in training) is used at test so effects are not prompt-template overfitting; injection counts are logged and a memorization check (verbatim-completion rate) is reported. Natural validation set: naturally-occurring cross-lingual factual disagreements (e.g. entities with language-divergent Wikipedia values) and natural per-language polysemy sense preferences, with independently verifiable answers, evaluated identically. Models: decoder-only GPT-NeoX/Pythia architecture trained from scratch at 160M and 410M parameters; all weights trainable; context 2048, AdamW, peak LR 6e-4 with 10% warmup and cosine decay, ~0.5M-token batches, 3 seeds (0,1,2). Training schedule is stated precisely and TOTAL OPTIMIZER STEPS AND COMPUTE ARE EQUALIZED across conditions: each run trains for the same number of steps on the same total tokens; 'late' means the target language's tokens are confined to the final third of the fixed schedule (so English-only pretraining does not buy the dominant language extra total compute; the dominant language's own token budget is matched across conditions). Acquisition-order conditions: (i) SIMULTANEOUS -- all four languages interleaved from step 0; (ii) SEQUENTIAL-LATE -- English trained alone first, target languages introduced only in the final third; (iii) SEQUENTIAL-EARLY -- target languages first, English introduced late; (iv) TOKEN-CONTROL -- as SEQUENTIAL-LATE but the late target language receives 2x tokens, dissociating lateness from exposure. Additional baselines controlling alternative accounts: (v) SHUFFLED-DOMINANT -- SEQUENTIAL-LATE but the dominant language's divergent-fact objects are shuffled random, so any inheritance cannot be 'the correct shared answer'; (vi) MONOLINGUAL-THEN-JOINT -- English-only then all languages jointly (curriculum control); (vii) NO-CONFLICT -- late language given EXCLUSIVE facts with no conflicting dominant-language fact, isolating conflict-driven inheritance from generic late-learning deficits. Power: injected-item counts (300/120/60) and 3 seeds x 2 sizes are set from a pilot so a 15 pp Parasitism-Score difference is detectable at 80% power (per-item binomial + seed-level bootstrap CIs reported); all injected items are used. Reporting: all Parasitism Scores are reported PER LANGUAGE with bootstrap uncertainty (not only averaged), since the claim depends on typological/script distance.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- behavioral parasitism is diagnosable, including inherited false beliefs): tests whether a late-introduced language's answers track the dominant language's idiosyncratic outputs rather than its own injected ground truth. Data: the 300 divergent facts (incl. the false-in-dominant subset), 120 polysemy items, 60 reasoning-quirk items, plus the natural validation set; all used; evaluated on held-out templates. Systems compared: the SAME target language under SEQUENTIAL-LATE vs SIMULTANEOUS vs SEQUENTIAL-EARLY vs NO-CONFLICT vs SHUFFLED-DOMINANT. Decisive metric: Parasitism Score = fraction of a target language's responses equal to the DOMINANT language's idiosyncratic output instead of the language's own injected ground truth (chance = 1/#answer-options, reported). Signature secondary metric (not obtainable from standard bilingual accuracy): asymmetric FALSE-belief inheritance = rate at which the late language reproduces the dominant language's FALSE fact despite its own matched, correct evidence. Convincing result: SEQUENTIAL-LATE Parasitism Score exceeds SIMULTANEOUS by >=15 pp averaged over seeds AND per-language for the far languages, with correspondingly lower own-ground-truth accuracy, and elevated false-belief inheritance; SHUFFLED-DOMINANT reproduces the inheritance pattern (ruling out 'inherited the true answer'); NO-CONFLICT shows the late language CAN learn its own exclusive facts (ruling out generic late-learning failure). Indecision band: a 5-15 pp gap = weak/partial parasitism; <5 pp refutes behavioral diagnosability for that language. Negative result (no gap, or SIMULTANEOUS >= LATE, or NO-CONFLICT equally impaired) undercuts the central claim.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- order, not token count): tests whether parasitism is set by acquisition order rather than exposure. Systems compared: SEQUENTIAL-LATE vs TOKEN-CONTROL (late language 2x tokens) vs SIMULTANEOUS, matched language and size, plus MONOLINGUAL-THEN-JOINT. Decisive metric: Parasitism Score of the late language, per language. Convincing result: TOKEN-CONTROL stays within 5 pp of SEQUENTIAL-LATE and remains >=15 pp above SIMULTANEOUS -- doubling tokens does not rescue autonomy, so order dominates exposure; this directly challenges the assumption that equal token counts yield equitable representation. Indecision band: extra tokens closing 5-10 pp = mixed account; closing >10 pp = exposure-driven, refuting H3. Negative result cleanly falsifies the order-over-count claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- parasitic vs autonomous representation, correlational): tests whether a late language shares more of the dominant language's concept/knowledge substrate than an early/joint one. Data: divergent-fact and polysemy items. Systems compared: cross-language (target, dominant) overlap under LATE vs EARLY vs SIMULTANEOUS. Decisive metric: representational overlap = mean of (linear concept-probe cross-decoding accuracy, normalised) and CKA between target and dominant mid-layer representations of the same concept; plus knowledge-locus overlap (Jaccard of the layers/positions a causal trace assigns a divergent fact to). Directedness (not symmetric sharing) is checked by comparing target->dominant vs dominant->target decoding asymmetry. Convincing result: LATE overlap exceeds SIMULTANEOUS by >=0.15 (shared 0-1 scale) AND is asymmetric (late depends on dominant more than vice versa). Indecision band: 0.05-0.15 = suggestive; <0.05 = no representational parasitism. Negative result weakens the mechanistic reading of H1.

Experiment 4 (H1 -- functional parasitism, causal): tests whether a late language's answer is causally driven by the dominant language's representation. Data: divergent-fact items where target and dominant answers differ. Model: the 410M runs. Cross-language patching correspondence: because scripts/tokenizations differ, we patch at the concept representation over the POOLED concept-span (last-token-of-concept and mean-pooled variants both reported), align layers by relative depth, and time-align at the answer-decision position; controls include a same-language null patch (identity), a random-direction/norm-matched patch, and a non-divergent (shared-fact) specificity patch. Method: activation-patch the dominant-language mid-layer concept/knowledge representation into the target-language forward pass and measure whether the target answer flips to the dominant value; reverse-patch (target into dominant) as a directed control. Systems compared: LATE-target vs EARLY-target flip rate under identical patching. Decisive metric: causal flip rate. Convincing result: LATE flip rate exceeds EARLY by >=20 pp AND exceeds all null/random controls, establishing directed functional routing through the dominant substrate. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = partial; <8 pp = no causal dependence (Exp. 3 overlap epiphenomenal). Negative result refutes the causal core of H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. From-scratch small-model training may not capture behaviors of large production LLMs; we use several sizes and controlled corpora and frame findings as mechanism-in-a-controlled-setting (a 'petri dish' as in Beyond the Rosetta Stone), complemented by the natural cross-lingual-disagreement validation set so results speak beyond synthetic injections. 2. Injected idiosyncrasies are artificial; the natural-data validation and held-out-template evaluation address prompt-template overfitting and ecological validity. 3. Parasitism could be confounded with sheer exposure or with generic late-learning deficits; the token-count control (Exp. 2), the NO-CONFLICT baseline (late-exclusive facts), and the SHUFFLED-DOMINANT baseline are designed to dissociate directed inheritance from exposure, generic lateness, and 'inheriting the correct answer'. 4. Probe overlap/CKA are correlational and symmetric; the directed activation-patching flip test with null/random/reverse controls (Exp. 4) is required to establish functional, directed parasitism (distinct from ordinary shared representation). 5. English-only pretraining could give the dominant language an optimization advantage; total steps, total tokens, and the dominant-language token budget are equalized across conditions to remove this confound. 6. Cross-script patching correspondence is nontrivial; we align by relative depth and concept-span position, report both last-token and pooled variants, and validate with identity/null patches. 7. Language selection drives the distance analysis; we report per-language results with uncertainty rather than only averages and check robustness to alternative language choices. 8. Reversibility of parasitism is left to future work and is not claimed here, since the current design does not include a specified corrective-intervention experiment. 9. Compute stays within academic reach at 160M-410M scale with modest corpora; we prioritize a minimal factorial over an exhaustive grid.
